title: Storage — User Documentation  documentation

title: Storage — User Documentation  documentation
text: Each research group can request access to 5TB of shared storage under /groups/PI_netid , where members can create subdirectories as needed. Additional storage beyond 5TB is available for a cost.

title: Storage — User Documentation  documentation
text: A snapshot means that we are able to reproduce a complete copy of the data as it existed at a previous point in time.  Snapshots are stored offsite from the primary data center. The CRC provides up to 30 days of recovery.

title: Storage — User Documentation  documentation
text: For each home, group and /goldfs directory an automatic snapshot is created every day. The one weekly and the three daily snapshots from the last 3 days  can be found under the following directories (the YYYY-MM-DD part of the path refers to the format of the date):

title: Storage — User Documentation  documentation
text:
# The daily and weekly snapshots for home directories are under: /users/.snapshot/daily.YYYY-MM-DD_0010/netid
/users/.snapshot/weekly.YYYY-MM-DD_0015/netid # The daily and weekly snapshots for group directories are under: /groups/.snapshot/daily.YYYY-MM-DD_0010/PI_netid
/groups/.snapshot/weekly.YYYY-MM-DD_0015/PI_netid

title: Storage — User Documentation  documentation
text: Every compute host has a local disk which contains the OS and a small amount of space available to users. This local disk will normally be faster for higher I/O bound jobs, in addition to relieving network congestion to the other networked file systems available.

title: Storage — User Documentation  documentation
text: The amount of storage available on the local disk varies by which machine the job is running on. Some note:

title: Storage — User Documentation  documentation

text: All activity performed on the CRC infrastructure occurs on remote servers, this requires an ssh (Secure Shell) connection to a head node at the very least. Below are instructions for creating an ssh session to a head node specific to each popular OS.

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: For more information on the Public head nodes see the Proper Front End Usage page.

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: Note

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: Most distributions of Linux are shipped with a terminal available. Most likely, ssh will already be installed. Open a terminal, the process for doing so can very from distro to distro. Popular key-bindings are “CTRL + Alt + T”, or “Alt + F2”. From here you can simply use the ssh command to connect:

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: ssh netid@crcfe01.crc.nd.edu

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: If you plan on using a GUI (Graphical User Interface), you will need to forward an X connection to our servers. To do so, use the -Y flag to pass trusted X11 connections.

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: ssh -Y netid@crcfe01.crc.nd.edu

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: As macOS is a form of Unix , there is an included terminal application. Open the Launchpad and search for “Terminal”. Once you open the “Terminal” program you will have a shell in front of you. From here, you can use the ssh command.

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: ssh netid@crcfe02.crc.nd.edu

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: If you plan on using a GUI (Graphical User Interface), you will need to first download a program called XQuartz . Go to the XQuartz download page . It will install like most other macOS applications.

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: Once XQuartz is installed, you can use the -Y flag to ssh within a terminal to connect to a head node.

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: ssh -Y netid@crcfe01.crc.nd.edu

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
text: Note

title: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation

heading_path: Connecting to CRC Servers — User Documentation  documentation

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: The University of Notre Dame has a Condor pool which harnesses the idle computational cycles from workstations and servers all over campus to run batch jobs. Condor provides access to over 20,000 cores.  The Condor pool is maintained by the Notre Dame Cooperative Computing Lab (CCL) and CRC; most of the information in this article is taken directly from the CCL website .

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Visual Status of the ND Condor Pool 
text: ND Condor Utilization Matrix

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: Short Course In Data Centric Computing

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: Condor is a distributed batch computing system used at many institutions around the world. Condor allows many users to share their computing resources, thus giving everyone access to more computing power than any one person could afford to buy. In particular, Condor is good at harnessing idle cycles from under-used servers.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: Users that submit jobs to Condor can specify their own requirements on what machines to use. You can require the use of one particular machine, or any from a particular cluster, or any with a certain amount of memory or processor type. Of course, if you are borrowing machines owned by other people, then you must accept the possibility that some jobs may be kicked off and must run elsewhere.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: For more information about Condor, please visit the Condor project page at:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: https://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/ .

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: https://research.cs.wisc.edu/htcondor/ .

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: Log into condorfe.crc.nd.edu to submit jobs.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text:
To submit a batch job to Condor, you must create a submission file
and then run the condor_submit command.  Try creating this
sample submit file in /tmp/YOURNAME/test.submit .

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text:
universe = vanilla executable = /bin/echo arguments = hello condor output = test.output should_transfer_files = yes when_to_transfer_output = on_exit log = test.logfile
queue

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: Now, to submit the job to Condor, execute:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text:
cd /tmp/YOURNAME
condor_submit test.submit
Submitting job ( s ) ... 1 job ( s ) submitted to cluster 2 .

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text:
Once the job is submitted, you can use condor_q to look at the status
of the jobs in your queue.  If you run condor_q quickly enough,
you will see your job idle:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: -- Submitter: hedwig.cse.nd.edu : < 129 .74.154.241:33593> : hedwig.cse.nd.edu ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST PRI SIZE CMD 2 .0 dthain 8 /26 17 :21 0 +00:00:00 I 0 0 .0 echo hello world

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: If you job remains in state I ‘idle’ for a significant amount of time you should check to see why it has not started.  There is most likely a problem matching your request with an available resource which will be shown with the following command.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: condor_q yourjobnumberhere -better-analyze

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: The command below shows the relative priority of everyone who has recently run jobs.  Those with lower priority numbers have their waiting jobs start before others.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: condor_userprio

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: If you decide to cancel a job, use condor_rm and the job id:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text:
condor_rm 2 .0
Job 2 .0 marked for removal.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: Note

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: Getting Started With Condor at Notre Dame 
text: Despite what the Condor manual says, you will NOT receive email when a job is complete.  This feature has been disabled at Notre Dame due to our email security configuration.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: Because you will certainly want to run many jobs at once via Condor, you can easily modify your submit file to run a program with tens or hundreds of variations.  Change the queue command to queue several jobs at once, and the $(PROCESS) macro to modify the parameters with the job number.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text:
universe = vanilla executable = /bin/echo arguments = hello $( PROCESS ) output = test.output. $( PROCESS ) error = test.error. $( PROCESS ) should_transfer_files = yes when_to_transfer_output = on_exit log = test.logfile
queue 10

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: Now, when you run condor_submit, you should see something like this:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text:
condor_submit test.submit
Submitting job ( s ) .......... 10 job ( s ) submitted to cluster 9 .

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: Note in this case that “cluster” means “a bunch of jobs”, where each job is named 9.0, 9.1, 9.2, and so forth.  In this next example, condor_q shows that cluster 9 is halfway complete, with job 9.5 currently running.

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text:
condor_q

-- Submitter: hedwig.cse.nd.edu : < 129 .74.154.241:33593> : hedwig.cse.nd.edu ID OWNER SUBMITTED RUN_TIME ST PRI SIZE CMD 9 .5 dthain 8 /26 17 :46 0 +00:00:01 R 0 0 .0 echo hello 5 9 .6 dthain 8 /26 17 :46 0 +00:00:00 I 0 0 .0 echo hello 6 9 .7 dthain 8 /26 17 :46 0 +00:00:00 I 0 0 .0 echo hello 7 9 .8 dthain 8 /26 17 :46 0 +00:00:00 I 0 0 .0 echo hello 8 9 .9 dthain 8 /26 17 :46 0 +00:00:00 I 0 0 .0 echo hello 9

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: The condor pool is configured to enable dynamic slots. Therefore, if you want to submit multi-threaded or multicore SMP Condor jobs (e.g. using OpenMP), you can add below lines in your Condor job script:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: ... environment = OMP_NUM_THREADS = 4 ; LD_LIBRARY_PATH = ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH } request_cpus = 4 ...

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: For example, if you compile below hellow_world.c:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: #include <omp.h> #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> int main ( int argc, char *argv []) { int nthreads, tid ; /* Fork a team of threads giving them their own copies of variables */ #pragma omp parallel private(nthreads, tid) { /* Obtain thread number */ tid = omp_get_thread_num () ; printf ( "Hello World from thread = %d\n" , tid ) ; /* Only master thread does this */ if ( tid == 0 ) { nthreads = omp_get_num_threads () ; printf ( "Number of threads = %d\n" , nthreads ) ; } } /* All threads join master thread and disband */ }

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: with

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: icc -openmp hello_world.c -o hello_world.x

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: and then submit your Condor job script with

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: executable = hello_world.x

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: and above options, then you will get an output, for example, like:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
heading_path: To Submit Multicore SMP jobs to the ND Condor Pool 
text: Hello World from thread = 0 Hello World from thread = 1 Hello World from thread = 3 Hello World from thread = 2 Number of threads = 4

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: Following is a Condor submission script template for running Matlab with 4 cores:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text:
universe = vanilla getenv = true executable = Path_to_your_executable_file/executable.sh output = test.output error = test.error request_cpus = 4 should_transfer_files = yes when_to_transfer_output = on_exit log = logfile
queue 10

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: with ‘executable.sh’:

title: HTCondor — User Documentation  documentation
text: #!/bin/bash if [ -r /opt/crc/Modules/current/init/bash ] ; then source /opt/crc/Modules/current/init/bash fi module load matlab # If needed, specify the location of additional .m files.  Note that Condor must be able to read this directory. export MATLABPATH = /path/to/your/matlab/files #  Substitute your ID below to ensure Matlab can write configuration files to a unique directory: export MATLAB_PREFDIR = /tmp/netid export TMPDIR = /tmp/netid # Determine the full path to a matlab version export MLAB = ` which matlab ` ${ MLAB } -nodisplay -nosplash -nojvm -r "myFunction(' $1 ');exit"
